extracted.intended_audience: nonprofit grant writers and organizations seeking grant funding
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for nonprofit organizations and grant writers on common mistakes to avoid when preparing grant proposals to increase chances of securing funding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Starting before you’re truly grant ready
rubrics_metrics.description: Grant writing success depends on a well developed application from a well prepared organization. That means you should never start applying for grants before your organization is truly 'grant ready.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure your organization has a robust fundraising plan outside of grant writing and is otherwise prepared to compete. Consider multiple readiness factors before applying; avoid jumping into applications prematurely because underprepared organizations (e.g., those lacking diversified fundraising) will struggle to win grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not aligning with the funder
rubrics_metrics.description: All funders publish their priorities and interests when it comes to grant making. One of the biggest grant writing mistakes is to overlook certain details of these guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully read a grantmaker’s guidelines, website, IRS Form 990s, and any other published information before applying. If unclear, call the foundation to learn more about their priorities to confirm alignment before submitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing weak goals and objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Goals and objectives are a critical part of any grant application. Skimping on this section would be one of the biggest grant writing mistakes you can make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn and apply the basics of writing clear, specific, measurable goals and objectives. Treat this section as essential: define expected outcomes, measurable indicators, timelines, and the link between activities and desired results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failing to develop funder relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing strong funder relationships is a critical part of grant writing success. Long-term relationships mean long-term funding for your organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize relationship-building especially with foundation and corporate funders (less so for government grants). Opportunities include calling the funder before you apply, keeping the funder informed of organizational changes, and following up if you do not receive the grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficient research
rubrics_metrics.description: Thorough research is the lifeline of successful grant proposals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research should include the funder’s mission and previous grants, the needs of the community you serve, and statistical evidence to support your project. Use research to justify need, design, and fit with funder priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglecting the budget details
rubrics_metrics.description: The budget is a critical component of any grant proposal. It must be precise and realistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for and justify every dollar requested in the narrative; ensure figures are realistic and match program activities. Review for math errors, allowable costs, and alignment with funder budget formats and restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Over-complicated language
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposal that is difficult to read or filled with jargon will undoubtedly undermine your credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear, concise, and compelling language. Avoid jargon and overly complex sentences so reviewers can quickly understand your need, approach, and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failing to plan for sustainability
rubrics_metrics.description: Funders want to know that their investment will have a long-term impact. Failing to address how your project will continue after the grant ends is a significant oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concrete plans for sustaining activities and outcomes beyond the grant period (e.g., diversified funding, partnerships, institutionalization). Explain realistic timelines and steps to sustain impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using a generic proposal
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using a one-size-fits-all approach. You must tailor each proposal to the specific funder and highlight how your project aligns with their values and goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customize language, priorities, and examples to the funder; explicitly show alignment with the funder’s stated interests rather than recycling generic applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of proper evaluation methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Your proposal should include a detailed plan for how success will be measured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific evaluation methods, metrics, and data collection plans that demonstrate accountability and commitment to achieving results. Describe who will conduct evaluation, frequency, and how findings will be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not providing supporting documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong letters of support and relevant endorsements greatly influence your proposal’s credibility. Not including these can be viewed as a lack of community or sector endorsement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include timely, relevant letters of support and endorsements that corroborate need, partnerships, and capacity. Ensure documents are from credible partners and directly support your application claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rushing the submission
rubrics_metrics.description: You must always review your proposal multiple times and consider having an outsider critique it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow sufficient time for multiple reviews, editing, and outside critique to catch errors and improve clarity. Avoid last-minute submissions; thorough revision increases the chance of success.
